| [LIT-194](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-194.md) v3 | Religion and Science | De Cruz (2017), <https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/religion-science/>. A survey, not an argument. It reports that the scholarly field rejects the conflict model the public holds, and it finds Barbour's four-way taxonomy (conflict, independence, dialogue, integration) influential but neither exhaustive nor exclusive. Its survey of five traditions shows the relation varies with creed and colonial history, and it describes the field fragmenting into claim-by-claim "science engaged theology". Its metaphysical content is concentrated in §1.2 (methodological vs ontological naturalism) and §3.1 (divine action under deterministic, chaotic and quantum physics; primary vs secondary causation; chance and providence). | Active — read in full 2026-09-26 ([NOTE-107](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-107.md)); worth reading as the standard orientation to the science–religion literature and as a map of the divine-action and naturalism debates; it is a survey, so its claims are only as strong as the works it cites, and it is written from within the (largely Christian) field it describes. |
| [LIT-466](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-466.md) | Palatable Conceptions of Disembodied Being | Shanahan (2025), arXiv:2503.16348. Asks whether consciousness talk can be stretched to disembodied, 2024-vintage LLM agents. Their time would be discrete and discontinuous, a string of unlike beads. Their "I" has two palatable referents, the model across conversations and a self confined to one conversation that "flickers into being with each user interaction", and we may slip between them. Such selves can be edited, copied and merged, and smeared across branching simulacra. Every candidate site dissolves, which Shanahan reads as Buddhist emptiness, and turns back on human selfhood. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-376](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-376.md)) in arXiv v3 (July 2025), the only text there is; worth reading as the one paper here that argues directly about what an LLM's self is, rather than whether it has one. Its answer: two conceptions are in play, a self sited in the model and "fleeting, flickering" selves sited in single conversations, and we may slip between them; every candidate site "dissolves upon close examination", and Shanahan takes that to the Buddhist conclusion that there is no inherent self, here or in us. It is avowedly "poetic", not literal, and its examples are invented usages, not data. |

The individualizing–binding split appears in only three of 19 national networks. | [LIT-507](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-507.md) | Moral psychology is relationship regulation: Moral motives for unity, hierarchy, equality, and proportionality | Rai & Fiske (2011), DOI-10.1037/a0021867. Relationship regulation theory: moral judgments are not about features of acts (harm, unfairness, impurity) but about whether acts fit the relationship model in force. Fiske's four relational models each carry a moral motive: Unity (communal sharing), Hierarchy (authority ranking), Equality (equality matching) and Proportionality (market pricing). The motives are universal; cultures differ in where they apply them. So violence, inequality and "impure" acts can be morally required, and purity and ingroup loyalty are one motive. A review, with no new data. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-405](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-405.md)); worth reading as the relational alternative to both Moral Foundations Theory and morality-as-cooperation, and as the source of the Equality/Proportionality split the MFQ-2 later adopted. It is a theoretical review with no new data. It agrees with morality-as-cooperation that morality exists to sustain cooperative relationships, and differs from it on purity (a Unity motive, the same motive as ingroup loyalty), on harm (violence can be morally required) and on the units (four relational models, not seven game-theoretic problems). |
